note.title: Working scientifically, safety and evidence
note.overview: Good chemistry is not just remembering reactions. It means asking a testable question, controlling variables, measuring safely, finding patterns and judging whether the evidence supports the conclusion.
learningGoals: Recall the precise Year 8 scientific vocabulary and symbols.
Apply the idea to an unfamiliar example rather than relying on recognition.
Use the command word, show working where needed and include every mark point.
mustMemoriseRules: A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk combines the chance of harm with its likely severity.
Change only the independent variable, measure the dependent variable and keep relevant control variables constant.
Accuracy concerns closeness to the true value; precision concerns how closely repeated values agree.
Repeatability uses the same person and method; reproducibility uses a different person or method.
Put the independent variable on the x-axis and the dependent variable on the y-axis, with quantities and units in headings.
A conclusion must describe the pattern and support it with data; an evaluation identifies limitations and specific improvements.

mustMemoriseVocabulary.meaning: something with the potential to cause harm
the likelihood and possible severity of harm from a hazard
a relevant factor kept constant for a fair comparison
closeness of a measurement to the true value
closeness of repeated measurements to one another
agreement when the same person repeats the same method
agreement when a different person or method repeats the work
a result that does not fit the overall pattern

workedExamples.prompt: A bottle is labelled corrosive. Explain one hazard, one risk and one control measure.
